title: Aluminum tensile strength
intro:
An aluminum alloy is sold with a mean tensile strength of **310 MPa**. A lab tests **12 specimens** from a new shipment (MPa, in the table below). σ is not known. Test H₀: μ = 310 against H₁: μ ≠ 310 at α = 0.05.

Find the t statistic, its degrees of freedom and the two-sided p-value. Give t to two decimals and the p-value to three decimals or more; the degrees of freedom are a whole number.

To use the Workbench: press **Copy the data**, press Ctrl+B, click **+ Data table** and paste (Ctrl+V). Choose **One-sample test**, set **Test** to *Mean, σ unknown (t-test)*, **Data from** to *Columns of a data table*, **Column** to the *MPa* column, **Alternative hypothesis** to *Two-sided (≠)*, **Significance level (α)** to 0.05 and **Null value (μ₀, p₀ or σ₀)** to 310. Ctrl+L brings you back.

Statistic.says: You divided by s, the spread of single specimens. The t statistic divides by the standard error of the mean, s/√n.

DegreesOfFreedom.says: That is n. A one-sample t-test has n − 1 degrees of freedom: one is used up by estimating the mean.

PValue.says: That is one tail only. H₁ says μ ≠ 310, so a t this far out on either side counts: double the tail area.
You took the area from the normal (z) curve. σ is not known, so t follows the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails.

hints: First x̄ and s of the twelve values (s divides by n − 1 = 11).
The standard error is s/√n. t = (x̄ − 310) / (s/√n).

The degrees of freedom are n − 1. The two-sided p-value is 2 × P(T ≥ |t|) in the t distribution with that many degrees of freedom: Python 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df), R 2 * pt(abs(t), df, lower.tail = FALSE).
